HgqjnS2N0VM.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qalam, Part 2: Verses 8-16
HgqjnS2N0VM.one_line: The ten traits the Prophet was told not to emulate in 68:8-16, and how flipping them gives his character.
HgqjnS2N0VM.summary: After recalling that the juz is about dawah, where victory means people entering the deen rather than conquering land, he reads verses 8-16 as a list of ten traits the Prophet is told not to emulate. He first explains why the Quran often teaches by prohibition: a red line leaves wide space to act, as the shahadah itself begins with a negation. The first trait, the denier who rejects evidence he finds convincing, takes most of the session. Muslims follow evidence, build iman on the universe, history and human experience rather than on reasons for each ruling, and then trust Allah's commands the way a patient trusts a qualified doctor. Religion cannot be inherited, and a good Muslim admits error, as a Syrian Quran scholar did publicly after twenty years and as Abu Bakr did with Umar. He then covers compromise of principle (with a sharp critique of politicians' silence on Gaza), lying and lack of integrity, gossip and talebearing (he refuses to hear any), stinginess, harming others, base conduct, harshness and shame of one's own identity. Flipping all ten yields the Prophet's portrait, which the audience is asked to aspire to.

outline.heading: Recap: dawah as the goal, victory as people entering the deen
outline.gist: Last week's verse set the Prophet upon great character. The juz is about dawah, and An-Nasr defines victory as people entering Allah's religion in crowds, not conquering land, owning things or one empire beating another.

outline.heading: Our causes are about injustice, not ownership
outline.gist: Muslims keep causes central because injustice occurred and the deen requires them to stay a voice of truth; the four opening surahs give the knowledge, ethical, spiritual and behavioural requirements.

outline.heading: Let the outcomes judge whose path is right
outline.gist: Allah knows who is guided, so Muslims need not fight over it: live your values and let the results decide. Fail to live them and people will think Islam failed.

outline.heading: Do not emulate: why the Quran teaches by prohibition
outline.gist: 'La tuti'' here means do not emulate, not only do not obey. A command restricts you to a few options while a prohibition draws a red line and leaves wide space, as in the hadith to avoid what he forbids and do what he commands as much as you can.

outline.heading: The shahadah begins with a negation
outline.gist: Tawhid is stated as 'there is no god' before 'but Allah', which is why it is weighty; he tells atheists they are already halfway there.

outline.heading: Number one: the denier who rejects what he finds convincing
outline.gist: Takdhib is not plain disbelief but saying no to what makes the most sense because of arrogance, envy, fear or a lost interest, and the Quran treats it as a grave sin.

outline.heading: Muslims follow the evidence wherever it leads
outline.gist: As in 'if the Most Merciful had a son I would be the first to worship', Muslims accept truth from anyone, even people they dislike, and are never asked to walk blindly or lie to themselves.

outline.heading: Establish iman by evidence, then trust the commands
outline.gist: Certainty in Allah, the prophethood and the Quran comes through evidence; after that clear commands are followed without a reason for each, the way a patient trusts a qualified doctor without needing a medical degree.

outline.heading: Iman is built on the universe, not on the reasons for rulings
outline.gist: A clever arguer might win a debate over why something is haram, and that changes nothing. Iman is built on the universe, history and human experience, not on why there are five prayers or the Prophet's marriages; a hadith he cannot explain does not shake it.

outline.heading: You inherit your race, not your religion
outline.gist: We are Muslim because Islam makes the most sense, not because we took it from our parents; everyone must study the evidence for a Creator, his communication and his messengers themselves.

outline.heading: Converts lose nothing: Islam returns them to their own prophets
outline.gist: Islam sees other faiths as once led by great men with a book from Allah and later corrupted, so a convert gains the authentic teaching of his own prophet and belongs to his people more.

outline.heading: Stop demanding a reason for every detail
outline.gist: Children learning maths and patients questioning every drug show the flaw: trust the maxims you verified and accept what follows, or go back and fix your iman at its root.

outline.heading: A Syrian Quran master admits twenty years of error
outline.gist: A leading Syrian Quran teacher of his generation defended a disputed tajweed point, a slight lip opening in the hidden mim, for twenty years, then publicly said he had been wrong; Allah raised his name after it.

outline.heading: A challenge should send you back to your own argument
outline.gist: Defending something because it is familiar or ours is not Islamic. A challenge need not change your mind on the spot but should send you to study your own argument, as Muslims hope a Christian will re-examine the Trinity.

outline.heading: Islam never asks you to switch off your brain
outline.gist: Faith built on evidence needs logic; do not take anything on trust from anyone, even family, and write down what spouses owe each other rather than relying on trust.

outline.heading: Not because of our forefathers: Islam has the superior argument
outline.gist: Quraysh asked whether he was better than his grandfather; following forefathers is no argument. We are Muslim because Islam holds the superior argument, not the reverse, so never force things to fit.

outline.heading: The first value: adherence to the truth, and the count-and-flip method
outline.gist: He will count the traits and flip each one, since the mirror image is the Prophet. The first is adherence to truth and evidence without ego, which is why he was chosen and why those like him succeeded around him.

outline.heading: Umar and the woman who corrected him from the minbar
outline.gist: Umar, known for stopping at the Book of Allah, said a woman calling out from the back was right and he was wrong, because her point seemed stronger in that moment, even though his view held on reflection.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr rushes to admit he was wrong
outline.gist: After a quarrel with Umar, Abu Bakr came running to say the fault was his; the Prophet defended him as the one who believed in him when no one else did.

outline.heading: The first prohibition the early Muslims heard
outline.gist: These were among the first commands ever revealed, so the first thing the Quran forbade was being someone biased who will not follow the evidence.

outline.heading: Number two: they wish you would compromise
outline.gist: Idhan is giving something up for a gain. Quraysh, though stronger, kept offering deals, even asking him to seat the slaves behind the nobles, and he conceded nothing, so the stories make him sound like the one with the upper hand.

outline.heading: Politicians stand for nothing: the silence on Gaza
outline.gist: Politicians say anything for a vote, and a man like Trump is sold as a practising Christian. They stay silent on the Holy Land while children are pulled from rubble because they fear Zionist pressure and Muslims have not built enough pressure.

outline.heading: The most principled should lead; instead we pick the lesser evil
outline.gist: The leader should be the most principled person in a group, as the Prophet was. Today voters settle for the least harmful candidate, the Middle East has open dictatorship and the West a hidden one with the illusion of choice.

outline.heading: Number three: the habitual swearer, a liar for gain
outline.gist: Hallaf is a figure of speech for the liar who swears and exaggerates to escape trouble or get something out of people.

outline.heading: Number four: mahin, the one without integrity
outline.gist: Mahin has no sense of his own dignity or word and will flatter anyone or change colour to get his way.

outline.heading: Number five: the slanderer who carries tales
outline.gist: Hammaz mashsha' bi namim carries words between people to make them hate one another; tales you cannot verify only ruin relationships, so namimah is among the worst social sins.

outline.heading: His own rule: refuse to hear any gossip
outline.gist: From early in his marriage he refused all gossip, even about himself. Become boring to gossips and they stop; backbiting is eating a dead brother's flesh.

outline.heading: Rise above it: people will always talk
outline.gist: Drop gossiping friends even if it leaves you alone for a while. No one throws stones at a dead tree; those who talk about you are often envious and later seek your friendship.

outline.heading: Who has time to watch other people's lives?
outline.gist: Commenting on how others dress and behave is not the conduct of focused, purposeful people; he would buy that spare time for an eighth day of the week.

outline.heading: Number six: withholding good
outline.gist: Manna' lil-khayr withholds a kind word, money, time or help again and again, out of a selfishness that wants others to get less so he stays ahead.

outline.heading: Number seven: transgressing against others
outline.gist: Once you harm someone's space, wealth, freedom or integrity only Allah can help you; you cannot remove the pain or return stolen time, and an apology is only a first step. Arrive on the Day with clean hands.

outline.heading: Number eight: athim, conduct the community sees as low
outline.gist: Athim is one who engages in behaviour the community regards as base and unethical, below high character.

outline.heading: Number nine: 'utull, the harsh whom people abandon
outline.gist: 'Utull is the heavy, rude person others leave feeling worse; Allah told the Prophet that had he been harsh even the companions would have scattered, so family and community will not stay with someone who yells.

outline.heading: Number ten: zanim, ashamed of his own identity
outline.gist: Zanim claims a lineage, family or identity that is not his because he is ashamed of his own.

outline.heading: Count the ten, flip them, and you get Muhammad
outline.gist: The opposites are adherence to truth, steadfast principle, honesty, integrity, reconciling people, generosity, gentleness, high character, ease with people and pride in one's identity, which is exactly who the Prophet was.

outline.heading: Wealth, children and the brand on the snout
outline.gist: The one who calls the signs ancient fables because he has wealth and sons will be marked on the nose for all to see.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: The passage is a list of ten anti-values whose opposites define the Muslim and the Prophet's character.

themes.label: Eman: faith, certainty, doubt
themes.note: Faith is built on evidence from the universe and history, not on reasons behind each ruling; once certain, commands are followed with trust.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Following the better argument and publicly admitting error is a mark of the Prophet, his companions and true scholars.

themes.label: Istiqamah: incorruptibility, steadfastness, moral integrity
themes.note: The Prophet compromised nothing despite weakness; lying and lack of self-respect are the opposite of integrity.

themes.label: Leadership, governance and institutions
themes.note: Leaders should be the most principled, yet today's politicians sell their values for votes and money.

themes.label: Palestine, Gaza and the suffering of Muslims
themes.note: Politicians stay silent while children are pulled from the rubble because the community has not built enough pressure.

themes.label: Guarding the tongue; speech and gossip
themes.note: Talebearing and backbiting ruin relationships; refuse to hear it and stop caring what people say about you.

themes.label: Selfishness, greed of the soul (shuhh) and selflessness
themes.note: Withholding good so that others do not get ahead of you.

themes.label: The unlawfulness of harm and protecting others
themes.note: Harm cannot be undone; come to the Day of Judgment with clean hands.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: Mirroring the ten prohibited traits reveals exactly who the Prophet was.

-vTw6595Ru0.speaker: adnan
-vTw6595Ru0.speaker_note: Sunday tafseer series in his own voice; refers to the series plan and his prior session on Al-Mulk
-vTw6595Ru0.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qalam, Part 1: Verses 1-7
-vTw6595Ru0.one_line: Opening Al-Qalam as the surah of values: the oath by the pen, the Prophet upon great character, and time exposing everyone's true values.
-vTw6595Ru0.summary: He places Al-Qalam as the second surah of Juz Tabarak, which he reads as the requirements for carrying Islam: Al-Mulk supplied knowledge, Al-Qalam supplies values and ethics. It is among the earliest revelations, and he notes how the first revealed verses, the meeting with Waraqah (whose name means paper) and a surah named the Pen all point to learning. He urges people to write and journal, since defining a value in a clear sentence is how an idea becomes a lived ethic, and he separates fixed, written values from fiqh rulings that change with time, place and person. In the verses he reads the oath by the pen as each person writing the book they will read before Allah, and as documentation driving human and Islamic civilization. He explains the denial that the Prophet is mad, the reward that is never spoiled by reminders, and the Prophet standing upon great character as a foundation, which is why he was chosen and why converts with good character excelled. The closing verses teach that time exposes values, so one need not argue or worry about those who wrong you.

outline.heading: Juz Tabarak as the requirements of carrying Islam
outline.gist: The cluster is about carrying Islam yourself and to others, since being a vehicle for guidance is a main reason to be Muslim. Its first four surahs cover knowledge, values, spirituality and behaviour; Al-Mulk gave knowledge, Al-Qalam gives values.

outline.heading: One of the very earliest revelations
outline.gist: Most scholars rank Al-Qalam second after Al-Alaq, so its phrases were the first the Muslims ever heard: its garden story was their first story and Yunus the first prophet mentioned to them.

outline.heading: The first revealed verses point to knowledge six times
outline.gist: Iqra' twice, the pen, 'allama and the verb to know: read here means reflect, contemplate and gather knowledge, not just recite a text.

outline.heading: Waraqah, whose name means paper, and a surah called the Pen
outline.gist: After the first revelation the Prophet was taken to Waraqah, who explained his whole mission; his name means paper, a seventh reference to knowledge, and the next surah revealed is named the Pen.

outline.heading: Writing is how things sink in: the Libyan memorizers
outline.gist: Typing does not stick but writing does; Libyan and Somali students memorize the Quran by writing it and win the big competitions, and concepts sink in the same way.

outline.heading: Structure a sentence to build a value
outline.gist: He asks people to stop the reels and journal: a word like honesty is abstract until you define it in a sentence, and structuring that sentence is half the work of building an ethic.

outline.heading: The Quran preserved because it was written
outline.gist: Over a thousand companions memorized it, but it reaches us down to every articulation because it was written from day one, on bones, wood and palm leaves when writing material was hard to find.

outline.heading: Defining honesty: a worked example
outline.gist: A notebook will not ruin the Amazon. Honesty means telling the truth when it is uncomfortable or costly, without being rude or blunt about people's feelings.

outline.heading: Values are written: the pens have been lifted
outline.gist: The pen symbolises that values are documented and fixed, as the Prophet said of decree that the pens are lifted and the pages dry.

outline.heading: Fiqh is dynamic, values are fixed
outline.gist: Rulings respond to time, place, person and circumstance, so a new Muslim's fiqh differs from a lifelong Muslim's; honesty, trust, loyalty, kindness and empathy are the same in any century.

outline.heading: Take rulings locally; differ on fiqh, never on values
outline.gist: This surah has almost no fiqh. Ask your local scholar rather than a sheikh in another country; scholars differ on wiping over socks by design, but no sheikh differs on honesty or justice.

outline.heading: A surah every Muslim needs
outline.gist: If he had to choose one surah for people to hear, it would be this one: its values speak equally to the imam, the lifelong Muslim and the new Muslim.

outline.heading: Nun: its recitation and the challenge theory
outline.gist: Nun takes six counts. The most accepted view of the opening letters is that they challenged the Arab poets with their own letters.

outline.heading: The opening letters as coding: a fourth dimension
outline.gist: Surahs sharing the same opening letters share a common thread. Beyond when a surah was revealed, where it sits, and what it does for you, the letters add a fourth dimension we do not yet fully grasp.

outline.heading: Allah's oaths carry content and need an answer
outline.gist: Allah never swears aimlessly: what he swears by tells a story before the answer comes, unlike our oaths by Allah or the Prophet's oath by the One in whose hand is his soul.

outline.heading: The oath by the pen: you are writing your own book
outline.gist: Every choice writes the novel you will read aloud before Allah, perhaps with others listening, with your motives and thoughts laid bare, so choose the story you want to read.

outline.heading: Documentation let humanity build on itself
outline.gist: Written history is scarce until the last millennium or so; once knowledge was recorded, people could absorb a whole civilization's rise and fall in hours and build on it.

outline.heading: Muslims led the boom of documentation
outline.gist: Muslims translated and extended Greek, Persian and Roman learning, Aristotle included, instead of burning it. Writing preserved the Quran exactly and saved the hadith, and narrators who lost their written records were not relied on.

outline.heading: Two readings of 'you are not mad'
outline.gist: The answer to the oath: either by your Lord's grace you are not mad, or, as he prefers, in spreading your Lord's blessing, the Quran, you are not mad.

outline.heading: Called mad, never a liar: forty years without a lie
outline.gist: Madness was the first accusation because Quraysh could not call him a liar after forty years in which no one close to him heard a lie, a rare thing that takes a certain personality.

outline.heading: Ghayr mamnun: a reward never spoiled by reminders
outline.gist: A gift repeatedly brought up becomes a burden, as the Quran warns against spoiling charity with reminders; the reward is free of being told you did not deserve it.

outline.heading: Allah makes you feel you earned it
outline.gist: The Quran attends to the psychological side of reward: whoever enters Paradise knowing it is Allah's bounty is made to feel he earned it, so the joy is complete, which one-word translations like 'unending' miss.

outline.heading: Values and ethics: the ethic is the value made visible
outline.gist: The answer to the oath has three parts, the third being 'upon great character'. A value such as empathy is one word; the ethic is how it shows up with each person, though some philosophers split them as individual versus community.

outline.heading: 'Ala: ethics as the ground you stand on
outline.gist: The Arabs pictured ethics as a foundation you stand upon, letting you hold your head high, see further and not lose your footing.

outline.heading: Chosen for his character; people are like minerals
outline.gist: He had great character before prophethood, and that is why he was chosen. The best of people before Islam are the best in Islam once they learn it.

outline.heading: Umar and Hamza: late converts who excelled through their values
outline.gist: Umar came six years late yet became central to the religion, and the seerah books give his and Hamza's conversions their own chapter, because their values were ready; those who lied and cheated take far longer to change.

outline.heading: Character, not ritual, defines your Islam
outline.gist: People who pray in the first row can still cheat in business. No one in the Quran is praised for ethics like the Prophet, so he is set as the role model to watch and learn from.

outline.heading: Maftun: the trial that shakes your foundation
outline.gist: 'You will see and they will see which of you is tried': a fitnah from Allah is a heavy trial that shakes who you are and can make you lose your footing.

outline.heading: Time exposes values, so don't worry about those who wrong you
outline.gist: The Quran declines to argue and lets time show. Anyone who cheats or mistreats you will have the reputation they deserve before they leave this earth; if they are good it was a slip Allah forgives.

outline.heading: You can't hide patterns forever: the thief's 'first time'
outline.gist: A thief who swore it was his first theft was told Allah never exposes someone at the first slip. This is for your own self-check, not for judging those who are exposed.

outline.heading: Your Lord knows best who strayed: let time show it
outline.gist: The Quran does not argue with the disbelievers; it states the Prophet's character and lets time judge, and fourteen centuries later people still try to emulate him.

outline.heading: Remembered for values, not possessions
outline.gist: Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab are remembered only for opposing him. No one remembers your house or degrees; your values are what remain and testify for or against you.

22:41.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ إِن مَّكَّنَّٰهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ أَقَامُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتَوُاْ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَمَرُواْ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَنَهَوۡاْ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِۗ وَلِلَّهِ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
22:41.en: Those who, if We give them power in the land, establish worship and pay the poor-due and enjoin kindness and forbid iniquity. And Allah's is the sequel of events

31:17.ar: يَٰبُنَيَّ أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأۡمُرۡ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَٱنۡهَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَٱصۡبِرۡ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَصَابَكَۖ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ عَزۡمِ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
31:17.en: O my dear son! Establish worship and enjoin kindness and forbid iniquity, and persevere whatever may befall thee. Lo! that is of the steadfast heart of things

3:159.ar: فَبِمَا رَحۡمَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ لِنتَ لَهُمۡۖ وَلَوۡ كُنتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ ٱلۡقَلۡبِ لَٱنفَضُّواْ مِنۡ حَوۡلِكَۖ فَٱعۡفُ عَنۡهُمۡ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُمۡ وَشَاوِرۡهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَمۡرِۖ فَإِذَا عَزَمۡتَ فَتَوَكَّلۡ عَلَى ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُتَوَكِّلِينَ
3:159.en: It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee. So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult with them upon the conduct of affairs. And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah. Lo! Allah loveth those who put their trust (in Him)

5:105.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ عَلَيۡكُمۡ أَنفُسَكُمۡۖ لَا يَضُرُّكُم مَّن ضَلَّ إِذَا ٱهۡتَدَيۡتُمۡۚ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ مَرۡجِعُكُمۡ جَمِيعࣰ ا فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
5:105.en: O ye who believe! Ye have charge of your own souls. He who erreth cannot injure you if ye are rightly guided. Unto Allah ye will all return; and then He will inform you of what ye used to do

EC9O6DzHJqU.title: The Pledge of Al-Aqabah: The Third Article, Reforming Social Values (Part 2)
EC9O6DzHJqU.one_line: Every society has values: reinforce the good ones, push back on the bad, keep this distinct from dawah, and see how the Prophet reformed Arab values.
EC9O6DzHJqU.summary: His second khutbah on the third article of the Aqabah pledge, the Prophet's condition that Madinah accept a reform of its social values. He grounds the article in 'urf, custom, which jurists use as a secondary source of evidence, and in the word ma'ruf, the known good. Every society has values; Muslims should neither pretend otherwise nor try to erase them, but identify what they share, reinforce it in practice, and push back against the rest. He separates this from dawah: calling someone to Islam needs preparation, a relationship and finesse aimed at making them love Allah, while asking someone not to take a handicap spot needs only conviction, and mixing the two loses both. Al-Hajj 22:41 pairs ritual with reformed values. Values abandoned through silence are lost, which he says the confusion around gender shows, and Muslims, Arabs especially, are themselves known for rudeness and disregard for others. The Prophet kept the Arabs' generosity and loyalty but ended racism, female infanticide, usury and autocracy, beginning by consulting people himself. In the second khutbah he cites the warning that abandoning enjoining good brings punishment and unanswered dua, and laments the crime, abuse and dishonesty he sees in the community.

outline.heading: Opening
Returning to the third article: the status quo will not be accepted
outline.gist: Muslims misunderstand this concept and mix it with other things. The Prophet made it a condition of coming to Madinah: some values he would strengthen, explain and praise, others he would push against and remove; he was not coming to validate all of their values.

outline.heading: 'Urf: custom as a source of evidence
outline.gist: Beyond the four agreed sources, Quran, Sunnah, consensus and analogy, scholars use other sources when those are silent, and custom is one of them. The word ma'ruf literally means simply "that which is known".

outline.heading: Ma'ruf: the known good
outline.gist: Being an optimistic desert people, the Arabs used the bare word to mean what is known to be good and beneficial. So ma'ruf is about the norms of your society: the values you agree with you reinforce through behaviour, practice and reminders, and the ones you do not you push back against.

outline.heading: Every society has values
outline.gist: It is arrogant to imagine any people has no values: some write them into a constitution, others simply live them and you notice them over time. Muslims do not ask anyone to erase everything they have and take a new set.

outline.heading: Values work is not dawah
outline.gist: Rituals and acts of worship matter, but bringing people to them is dawah, which has its own art. The distinction exists because once you mix the two, one or both get lost.

outline.heading: Inviting to Islam versus asking him not to block a driveway
outline.gist: Calling a non-Muslim to Islam and asking the same man not to take a handicap spot or block a driveway are different acts done by different people. Not everyone is qualified for dawah: it needs preparation, education, a relationship, the right circumstances and finesse.

outline.heading: The goal of dawah is that they love Allah
outline.gist: The art of dawah is bringing people closer to Allah so they love Him. If you do not know how to do that, be a facilitator and bring someone who does; everyone has a role, but not necessarily the speaking role.

outline.heading: Values need only conviction
outline.gist: Upholding values needs no finesse or preparation: reinforce the ones we share, call out those who break them, and push back on the rest vocally, through advocacy, politics and the media. Both are fully required in the deen, and dawah is the fourth article.

outline.heading: Ritual and values together
outline.gist: In Al-Hajj 22:41 those given authority in the land establish prayer and zakat and command good and forbid wrong: both must happen. Luqman's advice to his son makes everyone responsible for values, though not everyone should be giving religious advice.

outline.heading: Fewer fatwas, more basic decency
outline.gist: Stop passing on a shaykh's opinion as the only one when it is one among many acceptable views. Values are clear: respect, empathy, equality, kindness, standing in line, leaving your car where it blocks no one, the basics of human decency.

outline.heading: Stop fighting for a value and you lose it
outline.gist: In one area of life the basics are already gone: people fear being fired over pronouns and no longer know how to define male and female or who may marry. Stop pointing things out and you lose them, so say plainly that no one may speak to or treat a child, a wife, a client or any human being that way.

outline.heading: Etiquette is itself a value
outline.gist: This is not a call to aggression: speaking to people in the best way is one of our values. Instead Muslims, Arabs especially, are known as rough and loud and as not respecting other people's space.

outline.heading: 'Me first, let the flood take everyone'
outline.gist: The attitude that only my getting through matters is not Islamic. Children must not grow up thinking they can bully others or answer elders disrespectfully; dawah and values overlap, but the Prophet and the Quran distinguished them.

outline.heading: Values are shared by humanity
outline.gist: No one needs to be Muslim to agree that people are equal and deserve the same rights and respect, which is why this is not dawah. When people lose their values they lose everything; the Arabs were generous and kept their word but were deeply racist.

outline.heading: What the Prophet ended
outline.gist: Racism, worse then than in today's worst gatherings, burying newborn daughters, a distorted view of women and usury were values he declared done with. Governance was another: everyone was to have a voice.

outline.heading: Ending one-man rule, starting with himself
outline.gist: Arabs sat before their chief and flattered him; no one's opinion mattered. The Prophet, who had revelation, began asking people what to do, because the Quran told him to consult them, and the change of value started with himself.

outline.heading: Our task: name the values and practise them first
outline.gist: Muslims in this country must identify the values here that are Islamic, be first to practise and teach them, and push back on the rest vocally, appropriately and with sound arguments. It is complicated, and only small silos of Muslims are thinking about it.

outline.heading: Those who clung to the old values lost their status
outline.gist: The Ansar understood that things would change: anyone who kept up tribal hostility, usury or drinking lost his standing. Here our basic values are threatened, and we must acknowledge it before we can change our reality.

outline.heading: Interlude
After Badr: wealth with a right for others
outline.gist: A change of value beyond zakat: wealth that comes in is not only for those who took part but strengthens the poor. The companions disliked it and said what they should not have, revelation told them not to quarrel over it, and they later admitted their conduct.

outline.heading: Command good, or your dua goes unanswered
outline.gist: In an authentic narration the Prophet swore that you will command good and forbid wrong, or Allah will soon send a punishment and then not answer you when you call on Him. Once values rot, what is the point?

outline.heading: White clothes, black heart: the dusty traveller
outline.gist: Praying in the first row dressed in white means nothing if the heart is black. The dishevelled traveller raises his hands to Allah while his food and drink are haram; values decide whether you touch haram when you are hungry or in need.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr corrects the reading of 5:105
outline.gist: Refusing haram in a financial pinch while fearing for your children is a value. Abu Bakr on the minbar told people they recite "you are responsible for yourselves" without understanding it, for he heard the Prophet say that if they do not command good and forbid wrong, Allah will punish them all.

outline.heading: Our community's failing values
outline.gist: Our basic values are being questioned and we are not upholding them: in his work with people he sees crime, domestic abuse, corners cut, untrustworthy dealings and disregard for law and order.

outline.heading: How can we ask for victory?
outline.gist: We keep asking Allah for success and victory while we cannot uphold basic decency, respect or empathy among ourselves. It has changed many times before and will change through people who care, but pretending all is well leaves our children questioning their values.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: Every society has a value system; Muslims reinforce the values Islam shares, push back on the rest, and lose their own values when they stop defending them.

themes.label: Commanding good and forbidding wrong (amr bil-ma'ruf)
themes.note: Abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil brings collective punishment and unanswered dua, and 5:105 is no excuse for silence.

themes.label: Dawah, outreach and representing Islam
themes.note: Dawah needs preparation, relationship and art because its goal is that people love Allah; it is distinct from upholding shared values, which everyone can do.

themes.label: Character and manners (akhlaq)
themes.note: Basic decency in lines, parking and speech; etiquette is a value, and Muslim roughness and selfishness are not Islamic.

themes.label: Seerah events and their lessons
themes.note: The Prophet kept good Arab values and removed racism, infanticide, usury and autocracy, consulting people himself and stripping status from those who resisted.

themes.label: Muslim identity and life in the West / Canada
themes.note: Muslims in this country must identify the shared Islamic values to champion and those to oppose with sound argument, because their own values are under threat.

themes.label: Jurisprudence rulings and how to approach fiqh
themes.note: Custom ('urf) as a secondary source of evidence and the meaning of ma'ruf as the known good.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah
themes.note: Crime, domestic abuse and dishonest dealings in the community show values are not being upheld; change is possible through people who care.
